title: Märchen von der Unke
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 105. Text from Wikisource („Märchen von der Unke (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 105 is not one story but three separate little toad-tales printed together under a single title; the break between them is abrupt enough that a reader expecting one continuous plot may think something has gone wrong partway through — it hasn't. The first tells of a child who shares its bowl of milk each afternoon with a house-toad that brings small treasures in return, until the frightened mother kills the toad, and the child, who had been thriving on the arrangement without anyone understanding why, sickens and dies without it. The second follows an orphan girl whose blue silk kerchief lures a toad out with a tiny golden crown; she keeps the crown instead of giving it back, and the toad, who would have brought her still more from its hoard if she hadn't, beats its head against the wall in grief. The third is only three sentences long, a scrap of dialogue between a child and a toad about a missing pair of ‘little red stockings,’ printed in a Low-German-flavored snatch and left about as cryptic in translation as in the original.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein kleines Kind, dem gab seine Mutter jeden Nachmittag ein Schüsselchen mit Milch und Weckbrocken, und das Kind setzte sich damit hinaus in den Hof.
sentences.l: There was once a little child, to whom its mother gave every afternoon a little bowl with milk and roll-crumbs, and the child set itself with it out into the yard.
sentences.i: There was once a little child, and every afternoon its mother gave it a little bowl of milk with crumbs of white bread, and the child would take it out and sit in the yard.
sentences.n: “dem” opens a relative clause in the dative: to whom. “Weckbrocken” are broken pieces of “Weck”, the white wheaten roll. The child stays grammatically neuter throughout, so German says “es” and “sein” — the tale never tells us whether it is a boy or a girl, and the English “it” keeps that open.

sentences.t: Wenn es aber anfieng zu essen, so kam die Hausunke aus einer Mauerritze hervor gekrochen, senkte ihr Köpfchen in die Milch und aß mit.
sentences.l: But when it began to eat, then came the house-toad crawling out of a crack in the wall, lowered her little head into the milk and ate along.
sentences.i: But whenever it began to eat, the house toad came creeping out of a crack in the wall, dipped her little head into the milk and ate with it.
sentences.n: “Unke” is the fire-bellied toad. A “Hausunke” belonged to the household in folk belief — a luck-bringing creature that must not be harmed, which is the whole plot of this piece. “anfieng” is anfing (anfangen); “mitessen” is separable: “aß mit”, ate along with.

sentences.t: Das Kind hatte seine Freude daran, und wenn es mit seinem Schüsselchen da saß, und die Unke kam nicht gleich herbei, so rief es ihr zu
sentences.l: The child had its joy in it, and when it sat there with its little bowl, and the toad did not come up at once, then it called to her
sentences.i: The child took delight in this, and when it sat there with its little bowl and the toad did not come at once, it would call out to her:
sentences.n: “seine Freude an etwas haben” — to take one’s pleasure in something. “zurufen” is separable: “rief … zu”, called out to.

sentences.t:
„Unke, Unke, komm geschwind,
komm herbei, du kleines Ding,
sollst dein Bröckchen haben,
an der Milch dich laben.“
sentences.l:
“Toad, toad, come quickly,
come hither, you little thing,
[you] shall have your little-crumb,
on the milk refresh yourself.”
sentences.i:
“Toad, toad, come quickly,
come to me, you little thing,
you shall have your morsel,
and take your fill of the milk.”
sentences.n: A rhymed call, geschwind/Ding and haben/laben. The last two lines drop the pronoun “du” and let the verb ending carry it; the bracketed “you” is supplied so the English line can stand. “sich laben an” — to refresh oneself upon. The idiomatic line here does not rhyme.

sentences.t: Da kam die Unke gelaufen und ließ es sich gut schmecken.
sentences.l: Then came the toad running and let it taste good to herself.
sentences.i: Then the toad came running, and ate with a good appetite.
sentences.n: “sich etwas gut schmecken lassen” is the set phrase for eating with relish — to let something taste good to oneself.

sentences.t: Sie zeigte sich auch dankbar, denn sie brachte dem Kind aus ihrem heimlichen Schatz allerlei schöne Dinge, glänzende Steine, Perlen und goldene Spielsachen.
sentences.l: She showed herself grateful too, for she brought the child out of her secret hoard all sorts of beautiful things, gleaming stones, pearls and golden playthings.
sentences.i: She showed herself grateful too, for out of her hidden hoard she brought the child all manner of beautiful things: gleaming stones, pearls and golden toys.
sentences.n: “heimlich” in older usage is simply hidden, out of sight (it belongs to “Heim”, home); the modern overtone of stealth is not wanted here.

sentences.t: Die Unke trank aber nur Milch und ließ die Brocken liegen.
sentences.l: The toad however drank only milk and let the crumbs lie.
sentences.i: But the toad drank only the milk and left the crumbs lying.
sentences.n: “liegen lassen” — to leave lying, to leave untouched.

sentences.t: Da nahm das Kind einmal sein Löffelchen, schlug ihr damit sanft auf den Kopf und sagte „Ding, iß auch Brocken.“
sentences.l: Then took the child once its little spoon, struck her with it gently on the head and said “Thing, eat crumbs too.”
sentences.i: Then one day the child took its little spoon, tapped her gently on the head with it and said, “Thing, eat the crumbs as well.”
sentences.n: “schlug ihr … auf den Kopf” is the dative of possession: struck her on *her* head. “Ding” is what the child called her in the rhyme, and here it is affectionate rather than scornful.

sentences.t: Die Mutter, die in der Küche stand, hörte daß das Kind mit jemand sprach,
sentences.l: The mother, who stood in the kitchen, heard that the child was speaking with someone,
sentences.i: The mother, who was standing in the kitchen, heard the child talking to someone,
sentences.n: German has no continuous tense: “sprach” covers both “spoke” and “was speaking”, and the English has to choose.

sentences.t: und als sie sah daß es mit seinem Löffelchen nach einer Unke schlug, so lief sie mit einem Scheit Holz heraus und tödtete das gute Thier.
sentences.l: and when she saw that it was striking with its little spoon at a toad, then ran she out with a billet of wood and killed the good animal.
sentences.i: and when she saw that it was striking at a toad with its little spoon, she ran out with a log of wood and killed the good creature.
sentences.n: “nach etwas schlagen” — to strike at something. “tödtete” and “Thier” are the 1857 spellings of tötete and Tier. The mother sees vermin where the child saw a friend; the tale makes no comment and simply lets the consequence follow.

sentences.t: Von der Zeit an gieng eine Veränderung mit dem Kinde vor.
sentences.l: From that time on went a change forward with the child.
sentences.i: From that time on a change came over the child.
sentences.n: “vorgehen mit jemandem” — to take place in someone, come over them; separable, hence “gieng … vor”. “Kinde” keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Es war, so lange die Unke mit ihm gegessen hatte, groß und stark geworden, jetzt aber verlor es seine schönen rothen Backen und magerte ab.
sentences.l: It had, so long as the toad had eaten with it, grown big and strong, now however it lost its beautiful red cheeks and wasted away.
sentences.i: As long as the toad had eaten with it, it had grown big and strong; but now it lost its fine red cheeks and wasted away.
sentences.n: “abmagern” — to grow lean, waste away (separable: magerte ab). “rothen” is the 1857 spelling of roten. “Backen” here are cheeks — the noun, not the verb “backen”, to bake.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so fieng in der Nacht der Todtenvogel an zu schreien,
sentences.l: Not long, and in the night the death-bird began to cry,
sentences.i: It was not long before the death-bird began to cry in the night,
sentences.n: “Nicht lange, so …” is a compressed way of saying “it was not long before …”. The “Todtenvogel” (modern Totenvogel) is the owl, whose call was held to announce a death in the house.

sentences.t: und das Rothkelchen sammelte Zweiglein und Blätter zu einem Todtenkranz, und bald hernach lag das Kind auf der Bahre.
sentences.l: and the little redbreast gathered little twigs and leaves for a death-wreath, and soon afterward the child lay upon the bier.
sentences.i: and the robin gathered little twigs and leaves for a funeral wreath, and soon after that the child lay upon the bier.
sentences.n: The robin covering the dead is old folk belief, and here it does the office of the funeral. “hernach” — afterwards (archaic).

sentences.t: Ein Waisenkind saß an der Stadtmauer und spann, da sah es eine Unke aus einer Öffnung unten an der Mauer hervor kommen.
sentences.l: An orphan child sat at the town wall and spun, there saw it a toad come out of an opening low down in the wall.
sentences.i: An orphan child sat by the town wall spinning, and saw a toad come out of an opening low down in the wall.
sentences.n: The second of the three little toad-stories gathered under this one title begins here; they are not one continuous plot, and the tale does not join them up. “spann” is from “spinnen”, to spin.

sentences.t: Geschwind breitete es sein blau seidenes Halstuch neben sich aus, das die Unken gewaltig lieben und auf das sie allein gehen.
sentences.l: Quickly spread it its blue silken neckcloth out beside itself, which the toads mightily love and onto which they alone will go.
sentences.i: Quickly she spread her blue silk neckerchief out beside her — a thing toads love mightily, and the only thing they will step onto.
sentences.n: “ausbreiten” is separable: “breitete … aus”. The child is “das Waisenkind”, grammatically neuter, so German says “es” and “sein”; further down the tale calls her “das Mädchen”, and the idiomatic line uses “she” from the start. “lieben” here is the verb, to love (3rd pl.), not the adjective “lieb”, dear.

sentences.t: Alsobald die Unke das erblickte, kehrte sie um, kam wieder und brachte ein kleines goldenes Krönchen getragen, legte es darauf und gieng dann wieder fort.
sentences.l: As soon as the toad caught sight of that, she turned about, came again and brought a little golden crown carried, laid it thereon and then went away again.
sentences.i: As soon as the toad caught sight of it she turned back, came again carrying a little golden crown, laid it on the cloth and then went away again.
sentences.n: “alsobald” — as soon as (archaic). “brachte … getragen” doubles the verbs, brought it carried; German likes the pairing where English uses one verb and a participle. “kehrte … um” is umkehren, to turn back, with the particle at the end.

sentences.t: Das Mädchen nahm die Krone auf, sie glitzerte und war von zartem Goldgespinnst.
sentences.l: The girl took the crown up, it glittered and was of delicate gold-spinning.
sentences.i: The girl picked the crown up; it glittered, and was of a delicate spun gold.
sentences.n: “Goldgespinnst” is gold drawn out like thread, a web of gold; “Gespinst” belongs to “spinnen” — the girl at her spinning is answered in her own craft.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so kam die Unke zum zweitenmal wieder:
sentences.l: Not long, and the toad came back a second time:
sentences.i: It was not long before the toad came back a second time:
sentences.n: “zum zweitenmal” — for the second time; modern German writes zum zweiten Mal.

sentences.t: wie sie aber die Krone nicht mehr sah,
sentences.l: but when she saw the crown no more,
sentences.i: but when she no longer saw the crown,
sentences.n: “wie” again in its temporal sense, when.

sentences.t: kroch sie an die Wand und schlug vor Leid ihr Köpfchen so lange dawider, als sie nur noch Kräfte hatte, bis sie endlich todt da lag.
sentences.l: crept she to the wall and beat for sorrow her little head against it so long as she still had strength, until at last she lay there dead.
sentences.i: she crept to the wall and beat her little head against it in her grief as long as she had any strength left, until at last she lay there dead.
sentences.n: “vor Leid” — out of grief; “vor” gives the cause of something done without willing it. “dawider” is the old form of “dagegen”, against it. “todt” is the 1857 spelling of tot.

sentences.t: Hätte das Mädchen die Krone liegen lassen, die Unke hätte wohl noch mehr von ihren Schätzen aus der Höhle herbeigetragen.
sentences.l: Had the girl let the crown lie, the toad would surely have carried yet more of her treasures out of the hole.
sentences.i: If the girl had left the crown lying, the toad would surely have brought yet more of her treasures out of the hole.
sentences.n: The condition is made by putting the verb first — “Hätte das Mädchen …” for “if the girl had …”, with no “wenn” at all. “wohl” here is “no doubt, surely”, not “well”. “wohl” is the particle of assurance here — surely, no doubt.

sentences.t: Unke ruft „huhu, huhu,“ Kind spricht „komm herut.“
sentences.l: Toad calls “huhu, huhu,” child says “come out.”
sentences.i: The toad calls, “Huhu, huhu”; the child says, “Come out.”
sentences.n: The third and last of the little toad-stories, and the only one told in the present tense; the articles fall away as well, which gives it the clipped sound of a nursery rhyme. “herut” is the dialect form of “heraus”.

sentences.t: Die Unke kommt hervor, da fragt das Kind nach seinem Schwesterchen „hast du Rothstrümpfchen nicht gesehen?“
sentences.l: The toad comes out, then asks the child after its little sister “have you not seen Little-red-stockings?”
sentences.i: The toad comes out, and the child asks after its little sister: “Have you not seen Little Red-Stockings?”
sentences.n: “fragen nach” — to ask after, enquire about. “Rothstrümpfchen”, little red stockings, is a pet name for the sister; who she is, the fragment never says.

sentences.t: Unke sagt „ne, ik og nit: wie du denn? huhu, huhu, huhu.“
sentences.l: Toad says “no, I neither: how [about] you then? huhu, huhu, huhu.”
sentences.i: The toad says, “No, nor I either — and you? Huhu, huhu, huhu.”
sentences.n: The closing fragment slips into Low German: “ne” is nein, “ik” is ich, “og” is auch, “nit” is nicht. “ik og nit” leaves the verb out — “nor I either”. The bracketed “about” is supplied; the German has only “wie du denn?”. What the exchange is finally about is not recoverable from so short a scrap, and the Grimms print it as it came to them.

glossary.backen: die Backe — cheeks (pl.; not the verb backen, to bake)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also ‘he/she’ for neuter nouns such as das Kind, das Mädchen)
glossary.kehrte: umkehren — turned back, turned about (3rd sg. past; separable um-, the particle follows)
glossary.lieben: lieben — to love (3rd pl. present here); the adjective lieb, dear, is a different word
glossary.liegen: liegen — to lie (infinitive; liegen lassen: to leave lying, leave untouched)
glossary.ne: nein — no (Low German ne; not the reduced article ’ne)
glossary.nit: nicht — not (dialect nit; Low German and southern)
glossary.wohl: wohl — surely, no doubt (particle of assurance); also: well
